Jessica is a young writer from Brisbane, Australia. An avid consumer and lover of all things Film and TV, you will never tear her away from a screen. A tendency rooted from childhood, she once had dreams of becoming a member of the famed kids-band 'Hi-5'. Perhaps that's what pushed her to secure an education with a theater background. But now, as dreams evolved, her passions have turned to admiring performances from afar. Frankly, she's just grateful that she can put her binging skills to good use. Outside of work, Jessica recently completed her undergraduate double degree in Arts/Communications. Other than that, she spends most of her free time with family and friends, probably never forgetting to talk about the new movie or show she watched the day prior.

As we near the end of the year, it's time to acknowledge how 2026 has been a pretty good year for comedy. From shows about middle-aged crises and unconventional careers to dysfunctional families and messy friendships, television has produced plenty of reasons to laugh. Some of these have had us cracking up from beginning to end, while others masterfully balance their comedy with stories about grief, relationships, and the general disaster of being a person.

Better still, the best comedies of the year haven't necessarily been the loudest ones, either. They've found humor in awkward situations, deeply flawed characters, bizarre circumstances, and the uncomfortabilities of everyday life. So yes, while more comedies could very well bring us joy as the next few months go by, these are some of our favorites—as of right now.

6
'DTF St. Louis' (2026)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/dtf-st-louis-jason-bateman-linda-cardellini-david-harbour.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jason Bateman talking to David Harbour with Linda Cardellini standing between them in DTF St. Louis

blocks.x: Image via HBO

As Clark Forrest (Jason Bateman) and Floyd Smernitch (David Harbour) befriend one another after bonding over their stagnant marriages, the two decide to experiment with a local app intended for extramarital hookups. But tensions soon escalate into a toxic web of lies as Clark begins a secret affair with his new friend's wife, Carol (Linda Cardellini). Of course, things only get worse when Floyd suddenly turns up dead.

Don't let the show's color-grading confuse you. While it does place a murder mystery at its center, DTF St. Louis is much more interested in the absurdity of the people involved rather than crafting a conventional crime thriller. Indeed, the humor mostly stems from watching deeply flawed adults make spectacularly bad decisions, with Bateman, Cardellini, and Harbour playing their characters' loneliness and terrible judgment completely straight. It's dark, uncomfortable, and often very funny in the way only a comedy about sex, death, and middle-aged desperation can be.
Season 5
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/jean-smart-hannah-einbinder-4.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Jean Smart's Deborah Vance and Hannah Einbinder's Ava Daniels looking horrified in Hacks Season 5

blocks.x: Image via HBO Max

As Deborah Vance (Jean Smart) and Ava Daniels (Hannah Einbinder) return to Las Vegas, the two quickly discover a smear campaign has been mounted against the legendary comedian. And yet, despite that (as well as a non-compete gag order), Deborah is determined to defy the odds and chase a career-defining goal: selling out a stand-up show at Madison Square Garden.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F68a4112c5ceac-IMG_1589%20copy.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

While it may be its fifth and final season, Hacks never seems to run out of ridiculous problems for Deborah to turn into her personal crusade. Whether she's plotting around contracts, chasing the occasional milestone, or refusing to accept that the industry might not give her exactly what she wants, Deborah approaches every setback as though it were a declaration of war. Of course, Smart remains the show's shining weapon, able to make a vicious put-down or completely unreasonable demand land with impeccable comic timing, while the supporting cast gets plenty of room for its own chaos. And even after all these years, Hacks still knows how to make the entertainment industry feel like the funniest and most dysfunctional workplace imaginable. A truly great send-off to a masterful show.

'Margo's Got Money Troubles' (2026–Present)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/margos-got-money-trouble.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The family sitting around the living room in Margo's Got Money Troubles.

blocks.x: Image via Apple TV

Margo Millet (Elle Fanning) is a college dropout and aspiring writer whose life takes an unexpected turn when she gets pregnant by her English professor. Now, abandoned by her baby's father, she's left facing mounting bills with very few ways to pay them. As a result, Margo returns to the orbit of her unconventional parents, while also exploring increasingly unconventional ways of making money—including starting an OnlyFans account.

On paper, the premise could've easily become a grim story about single-parenthood, but Margo's Got Money Troubles somehow became so much more. For instance, rather than treating Margo's decision as a punchline or a cautionary tale, the show takes her sex work seriously and instead finds plenty of comedy in the situations surrounding it. And let's not forget how Michelle Pfeiffer and Nick Offerman make her parents' eccentricity an attraction in its own right (along with some other surprising appearances). Yet another win for AppleTV's growing catalog.

'Shrinking' (2023–Present)
Season 3
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/shrinking-season-3-jason-segel-harrison-ford-jessica-williams-cast-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Jason Segel sitting on bleachers with Harrison Ford, Jessica Williams, and the cast of Shrinking Season 3

Struggling to grapple with the death of his wife, Jimmy (Jason Segel) decides to abandon his professional boundaries as a therapist and start telling his patients exactly what he thinks—even if this creates chaos for his clients, loved ones, and himself. By the third season, Shrinking follows an overarching theme of moving forward as Jimmy and his tightly-knit circle are forced to brave other massive life transitions, whether that be about parenthood, illnesses, or careers.

Despite all the emotional upheaval, Shrinking remains one of television's funniest shows as its characters are spectacularly incapable of dealing with serious situations normally. Jimmy is still impulsive, intrusive, and very good at making other people's problems his own, while the show's found-family dynamic continues to generate plenty of wonderfully awkward and chaotic comedy. At the same time, the season gives its characters room to change, making the jokes feel more meaningful because there's actually something at stake beneath them. Funny, warm, and occasionally heartbreaking, season 3 has only left us begging for the next.

'Adults' (2025–Present)

A tight-knit, co-dependent group of twenty-somethings—Samir (Malik Elassal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele), and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen)—live together in Samir's childhood home in New York while attempting to figure out how to become functioning adults. Stumbling their way through life, their problems range from relationships to family, money, and the increasingly embarrassing realities of being responsible for themselves.

Adults truly stuck its landing this season as the show that perfectly encapsulates the Gen Z experience. For one, it completely commits to turning the mundane humiliations of your 20s into full-blown comic disasters. A fake ID, a dinner party, a workplace mistake, or even switching bedrooms can become the basis for an entire episode of increasingly stupid consequences. Season 2 also makes sure to give the ensemble more room to develop beyond the chaos, since the characters feel more like true friends rather than five people assembled solely to deliver punchlines. So let's renew the show for season 3, okay?

'Widow's Bay' (2026–Present)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/widow-s-bay-feature.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Matthew Rhys as Tom sitting at his office desk while hugging a folder to his chest in Widow's Bay

blocks.x: Image via Apple TV

Set in a fictional New England town, Mayor Tom Loftis (Matthew Rhys) is determined to transform the struggling community into a tourist destination. But his plans bring renewed attention to the town's strange traditions and long-buried secrets, forcing Tom and the locals to confront the unsettling forces that surround them.

After winning an egregiously record-breaking number of Emmys this year, it's not surprising that Widow's Bay has once again found itself on top. Rather than turning the horror into an excuse for constant jokes, the show lets the supernatural elements play out with genuine menace while also finding the comedy in the reactions of those caught within them. Rhys anchors the show with a stunningly straight-faced performance that makes the stranger moments even funnier. And of course, that humor is only amplified by the eccentric ensemble who all seem to have their own relationship with the town's bizarre history. The result is a rare horror-comedy that truly leans into the creepy and the absurd—and somehow makes both sides work.
